title: India and Japan Just Agreed to Build a Warship Antenna Together. It's Their First Joint Defence Project Ever.
excerpt: The UNICORN naval mast, 10 new cooperation pacts, and a yen-rupee settlement plan: the 16th India-Japan summit delivered more than ceremony.
body:
For two decades, India and Japan have described each other as "special strategic partners." On Thursday in New Delhi, they finally built something together.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi signed India and Japan's first-ever joint defence co-development agreement — a pact to jointly produce the UNICORN naval mast, a stealth antenna system designed for warships. The agreement was the centrepiece of the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit, which also produced pacts on artificial intelligence, critical minerals, energy, and a new roadmap for economic security.

"This project will open a new chapter in our defence technology partnership," Modi told reporters at Hyderabad House. "We will now jointly develop defence technologies that strengthen regional peace, maritime security, and the rules-based order."

## What is the UNICORN mast?

UNICORN stands for Unified Complex Radio Antenna. It is a stealth-optimised antenna system that integrates multiple communication, radar, and electronic warfare functions into a single mast structure on naval vessels. The technology reduces a warship's radar cross-section — making it harder to detect — while consolidating equipment that would otherwise require separate installations across the ship's superstructure.

The co-development project builds on a Memorandum of Implementation signed in November 2024 at the Indian Embassy in Tokyo. Japan has historically imposed strict self-restrictions on military exports, and the UNICORN project represents one of its most significant departures from that doctrine.

For India, the pact signals a deepening of defence-industrial ties with a partner whose precision engineering complements India's growing shipbuilding capacity. India currently operates the world's fourth-largest navy by tonnage and has ambitious plans to expand its fleet, including through indigenous aircraft carrier and submarine programmes.

## Beyond defence: the full ledger

The summit's outcomes extended well beyond the UNICORN mast. Modi said the two leaders signed approximately 10 memoranda of understanding spanning:

**Artificial intelligence**: A joint declaration on AI cooperation, with Modi noting that "the convergence of Japan's precision technology and India's software capabilities will give a new momentum and strength to global AI development." The agreement covers collaborative research, shared datasets, and mutual recognition of AI safety standards.

**Critical minerals and metals**: A cooperation framework for securing supply chains in rare earths, lithium, cobalt, and other minerals essential to the energy transition and semiconductor manufacturing. Both countries are seeking to reduce their dependence on Chinese-dominated supply chains.

**Energy**: A biogas initiative under which Japan will help India establish 1,000 biogas and organic fertiliser plants — a project that addresses both India's rural energy needs and its agricultural waste management challenges.

**Economic security**: A joint roadmap for economic security cooperation, the first such framework between the two countries. The document is expected to cover supply-chain resilience, technology protection, and coordinated responses to economic coercion.

**Yen-rupee settlement**: Perhaps the most commercially significant outcome was progress toward a yen-rupee trade settlement mechanism that would allow bilateral trade to bypass the US dollar. The framework, if implemented, would be one of the most significant de-dollarisation moves by two major US allies.

## The numbers

Bilateral trade between India and Japan reached $27.5 billion in fiscal year 2025-26. Japanese investment in India totalled $3.2 billion between April and December 2025. Around 1,400 Japanese companies currently operate in India — a number Modi called on Japanese business leaders to double within a decade.

Japan's pledged investment of over $61 billion in India over the next decade, announced during Modi's visit to Tokyo last year, makes it one of India's largest single-country investment commitments. Major projects include the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail corridor and a recent $1.6 billion acquisition of a 20% stake in Yes Bank by a consortium of Japanese investors.

At a business forum following the summit, Modi announced a "Japan Business Week" to be organised by the Prime Minister's Office, aimed at streamlining regulatory processes for Japanese companies entering India.

## The strategic context

The summit's timing was deliberate. It comes as both countries navigate increasingly complex relationships with their two largest strategic partners — the United States and China.

Washington's attention has been narrowing toward the Pacific and the Western Hemisphere, and its recent moves to negotiate an understanding with Beijing have left both Tokyo and New Delhi seeking stronger bilateral anchors. Japan, under Takaichi, has taken a notably harder line on China than her predecessors — she drew Beijing's criticism in November for saying that a Chinese use of force against Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival.

For India, the Japan relationship offers what the China relationship cannot: trust, technology transfer without equity demands, and strategic alignment without the baggage of a disputed border.

## What NRIs should watch

For the Indian diaspora, the economic dimensions matter most. The yen-rupee settlement framework could significantly reduce transaction costs for NRI remittances routed through Japanese financial institutions. The AI cooperation pact opens potential pathways for Indian tech professionals in Japan, where a severe demographic crunch has created growing demand for skilled workers.

And the UNICORN mast, while a niche military project, carries symbolic weight. It marks the moment when two of Asia's largest democracies moved from talking about defence cooperation to actually building something together — a shift from communiqués to co-production that neither country's partnership with China could replicate.
